subject: Climate & Environment
title: Greenland's Melting Ice Sheet
description: A short lesson to help you apply Greenland's Melting Ice Sheet.

hook.text: Greenland loses about 270 billion tons of ice each year. The rate is accelerating.

buildup.text: Meltwater pools on the surface, darkening the ice and absorbing more sunlight.

discovery.text: Some of that water drills through the ice sheet, lubricating its base and speeding glacier flow.

twist.text: Greenland alone holds enough ice to raise global sea levels by 7.4 meters if fully melted.

climax.text: Even partial melting would redraw every coastline on Earth over the coming centuries.

punchline.text: Greenland is melting from above, below, and within. All at once.

quiz.question: How much could sea levels rise if Greenland's ice sheet fully melted?

details.summary: Greenland's ice sheet holds enough water to raise global sea levels by about seven meters. It is losing mass at an accelerating rate, currently shedding roughly 280 billion tonnes of ice per year through surface melting and iceberg calving into the ocean.
details.whyItMatters: Greenland is the largest single contributor to current sea-level rise. Its freshwater discharge also threatens to slow Atlantic ocean circulation, with far-reaching climate consequences.
takeaways: Greenland's ice could raise sea levels by about seven meters
It loses roughly 280 billion tonnes of ice per year
Meltwater may weaken Atlantic Ocean circulation patterns

faq.question: How fast is Greenland's ice sheet melting?
faq.answer: Mass loss has roughly tripled since the 1990s. In extreme melt years like 2019, Greenland shed over 500 billion tonnes in a single season. Surface darkening from soot and algae accelerates melting by absorbing more sunlight.

faq.question: How much has Greenland already contributed to sea-level rise?
faq.answer: Since 1992, Greenland's ice loss has raised global sea levels by about 1.1 centimeters. While that sounds small, the rate is accelerating, and even partial melting over coming centuries would reshape coastlines worldwide.
